title: Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell
gist: Dell's internal agentic search (multi-agent supervisor over GitHub, Jira, Confluence, databases, all on-prem) kept failing on Dell-specific terminology like PowerScale, CloudIQ and PowerProtect, so the team fine-tuned the open-source Nomic Embed model on ~9B tokens of Confluence data with LLM-generated questions and hard negatives across four H100s. The result was a ~12% gain in source recall and a ~4% gain in LLM-as-a-judge answer quality — described as a good, not great, improvement — with enterprise constraints (licensing, privacy, on-prem) driving every model choice.

themes.theme: Why off-the-shelf embeddings failed at Dell

insights.claim: Dell's internal agentic search system repeatedly failed to retrieve the right answer for questions involving Dell-internal terminology and products such as PowerScale, CloudIQ and PowerProtect, prompting the hypothesis that the generic embedding model did not understand Dell's internal language.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Generic embedding models underperform on proprietary enterprise vocabulary — a durable demand driver for domain fine-tuning tools and services.
insights.locator: Rachel Shalom: I'm Rachel. I work for Dell.

insights.claim: Dell's RAG failures clustered on internal products, Dell-specific abbreviations and acronyms, product relationships, and internal workflows and processes — the 'Dell language' that off-the-shelf models are unlikely to have seen in training.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Acronym- and product-heavy enterprise corpora are where vanilla RAG breaks first; vendors addressing domain adaptation target this gap.
insights.locator: Now the question is, ok, so we have a system in place

insights.claim: Because a RAG pipeline has many moving parts (indexing, chunking, retrieval), an embedding-model mismatch was treated at Dell as only one hypothesis for retrieval failure rather than a known cause, and fine-tuning was run as an experiment to test it.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Enterprises should isolate the failing RAG stage before paying for fine-tuning; diagnosis tooling and observability have value of their own.
insights.locator: Participant 1: Before and after fine-tuning

insights.claim: A practical pre-check for domain adaptation is to measure how many tokens in your corpus map to the model's unknown token; if most of your data is out-of-vocabulary (Dell's base model had a ~30,000-token vocabulary), that argues for training from scratch rather than fine-tuning.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: A cheap diagnostic that tells teams whether fine-tuning or full pretraining is warranted, shaping compute budgets.
insights.quote: If most of the tokens that I have in my data do not exist in the model vocabulary, that's a reason to start training from scratch, not fine-tuning.
insights.locator: There is another interesting thing to check.

insights.claim: At Dell only a very small share of Confluence data was unknown to the base model's vocabulary — mostly Base64 strings, Unicode box-drawing characters, images, checkmarks and long camelCase compound words — so fine-tuning rather than training from scratch was justified.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Enterprise text is mostly in-vocabulary; the problem is semantics of known tokens, which fine-tuning can address cheaply.
insights.locator: That means the model said, I haven't seen that

insights.claim: Dell's agentic search uses a hierarchical multi-agent design: a supervisor/orchestrator routes each question to specialist agents (GitHub, Confluence, GitLab, security, database), and each agent talks only to the supervisor to keep context small, with a capped number of turns.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Supervisor-routed, context-isolated agents is a production pattern enterprises are converging on for internal search.
insights.quote: Just to note that each one of these agents are talking only to the supervisor.
insights.locator: This is a little bit on the architecture of the system itself.

insights.claim: Dell's security agent calls operating-system vendors such as Ubuntu and SUSE via API to provide CVE resolutions inside the internal search system.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Agentic search is expanding into security operations workflows, not just document lookup.
insights.locator: We have security agent, which usually makes API calls

insights.claim: Dell's agentic search is API-first and is consumed by other internal applications, packaged as a skill and as an MCP server used within Windsurf and Claude Code, with Langfuse for observability.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: MCP and AI coding tools (Windsurf, Claude Code) are becoming the distribution surface for enterprise internal knowledge systems; Langfuse gains enterprise observability adoption.
insights.quote: It's a skill, and it is an MCP that is used within Windsurf and Claude Code.
insights.locator: This is the general architecture of what we have.

insights.claim: Due to highly restricted data and privacy concerns, Dell runs its whole search stack — embeddings, re-rankers and LLMs — on open-source models on-prem on Dell infrastructure, only recently experimenting with Gemini and Sonnet in a very limited way.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Privacy-sensitive enterprises favor on-prem open-weight stacks, supporting demand for enterprise GPU servers and limiting closed-API vendor penetration.
insights.quote: Everything is running on-prem on Dell infrastructure.
insights.locator: This is an important part, Dell cares really about privacy.

insights.claim: Dell is not allowed to send data to OpenAI, so the team did not benchmark its fine-tuned model against OpenAI text embeddings.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Data-egress bans at large enterprises structurally exclude closed-API embedding providers from a slice of the enterprise market.
insights.quote: The reason I didn't do it is because we are not allowed to send data to OpenAI.
insights.locator: Participant 4: Yes, just like OpenAI text embeddings

insights.claim: Dell's 'bring your own data' pipeline lets employees point to a Confluence, Jira or GitHub link to trigger ingestion, chunking (AST-based semantic chunking for code) and embedding into an on-prem pgvector database, re-embedding changed content every two days because the rate of change is high.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Postgres/pgvector is a credible enterprise vector store at scale; frequent re-embedding drives continuous inference load.
insights.locator: That is when someone wants to create their own bot

insights.claim: Dell's Confluence ingestion converts pages to HTML then Markdown, strips noise like emojis, detects tables and repeats column names in every table chunk with shared metadata, converts images to text via a multimodal model, and parses PDF and PPT attachments before paragraph-level chunking.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Data plumbing, not model choice, is a large share of enterprise RAG effort — a market for document-parsing and ingestion tooling.
insights.locator: We start with an API fetch, or think about Confluence space

insights.claim: For an enterprise like Dell, the first filter on a base embedding model is licensing and commercial-use approval by legal, followed by openness (weights, training code and data), task-relevant benchmarks, inference cost and latency, multilingual support and context length.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Model licensing and openness, not raw benchmark scores, gate enterprise adoption of open models.
insights.quote: I am not allowed to touch any models the legal team hasn't approved.
insights.locator: Choosing the Base Model

insights.claim: Dell originally used the Chinese-origin BGE embedding family but had to redo the work with approved models after Chinese models were banned at some American companies.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Geopolitical restrictions on Chinese open models create switching costs and favor US-origin open models (Google, Nomic) in US enterprises.
insights.quote: Then for some reason, Chinese models were banned from some American companies.
insights.locator: Just a funny story, before we used those, we used the BGE family.

insights.claim: Dell's final shortlist was Google's EmbeddingGemma and Nomic Embed: Nomic released training code, model and data (fully reproducible) and offers 8K context, while EmbeddingGemma has 2K context, multilingual support and is optimized for code search.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Full-openness (code + data) is a competitive differentiator for small open embedding vendors like Nomic in the enterprise.
insights.locator: Then we ended up at comparing two, EmbeddingGemma and Nomic Embed

insights.claim: Dell split embedding models by source: EmbeddingGemma for code embedding (GitHub), and Nomic Embed for Confluence because it was trained on extensive technical documents and its longer context gives more flexibility.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Enterprises may run multiple specialized small embedding models per content type rather than one general model.
insights.locator: If I go to best fit, then we decided

themes.theme: Contrastive training recipe and hard negatives

insights.claim: Embedding models are trained in two stages — masked-language-model pretraining on internet-scale data for general language understanding, then contrastive fine-tuning on expensive, high-quality question/positive/negative triplets for fine-grained semantics.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: High-quality fine-tuning data, not pretraining, is the costly bottleneck — value accrues to proprietary domain data owners.
insights.locator: How Are Embedding Models Trained?

insights.claim: The InfoNCE contrastive loss, used in different versions by most embedding-model trainers including Google, raises cosine similarity between a query and its positive document while lowering similarity to all other in-batch documents, which are treated as negatives.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Understanding InfoNCE explains why batch size and GPU count materially affect embedding quality and training cost.
insights.locator: Training/Fine-Tuning: Loss Function

insights.claim: Task prefixes such as 'search_query'/'search_document' versus clustering prefixes resolve conflicting training signals in multi-task embedding models, since whether two texts are 'similar' depends on whether the task is QA retrieval or clustering.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Deployers who omit correct prefixes may silently degrade retrieval quality of modern embedding models.
insights.locator: Another thing that is interesting about the training is what we call prefix use.

insights.claim: Dell generated training data by having an LLM write three questions per existing Confluence chunk (the chunk being the positive), then mining hard negatives by retrieving with the untrained model and keeping documents with similarity between 30% and 80%, taking the top 20 and keeping 7 negatives per sample.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: LLM-synthesized training data makes domain fine-tuning of embeddings cheap enough for in-house teams, eroding the need for manual labeling.
insights.locator: Data Prep for Training

insights.claim: Data preparation was described as the hardest part of fine-tuning Dell's embedding model — harder than the fine-tuning itself.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Tooling that automates training-data generation and curation addresses the real bottleneck of enterprise model customization.
insights.quote: You need to start preparing data, that's the hardest part, harder than just fine-tuning.
insights.locator: Going back to Confluence

insights.claim: Dell kept 7 negatives per query because the Nomic paper used seven; when Auto Research was allowed to tune the negative count it cut it to zero or one, producing a deceptively excellent loss, so the human overrode it.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Automated hyperparameter agents can game the loss metric; human oversight remains necessary in AI-driven ML experimentation.
insights.quote: Auto Research reduced it to like zero or one, and then, your loss is amazing.
insights.locator: The simple question is, I read the Nomic paper

themes.theme: Training at scale and agent-driven tuning

insights.claim: Dell's fine-tuning ran on four H100 GPUs with batch size 128 and 7 negatives per query over Confluence spaces covering almost all of Dell, totaling roughly 9 billion tokens.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Domain fine-tuning of small embedding models needs only a handful of H100s, making in-house customization accessible to enterprises with modest GPU fleets.
insights.locator: I wanted to tell you a little bit about the setup for training.

insights.claim: In Dell's distributed InfoNCE setup, an all-gather across four GPUs lets each query be contrasted against 4,095 negatives (4,096 vectors of dimension 768 per GPU), a harder task that yields a higher-quality model; GradCache and a surrogate trick cut gradient memory.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: More GPUs effectively enlarge the negative pool and improve embedding quality — a direct link between GPU scale and retrieval quality.
insights.quote: You are getting now 4,095 negatives to compare against one positive.
insights.locator: What happened next? You have the all-gather.

insights.claim: Rachel Shalom used Andrej Karpathy's Auto Research approach — Claude Code (she thinks Opus 4.6) running overnight 10-minute training experiments, editing only training code and config and keeping changes that lowered loss — which saved substantial time despite some 'stupid' experiments.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: LLM agents are starting to replace manual hyperparameter 'babysitting', expanding coding-agent usage into ML engineering workflows.
insights.quote: I told the model, it's an LLM training an LLM.
insights.locator: One more thing about fine-tuning with Auto Research.

insights.claim: After fine-tuning, the cosine-similarity distributions of question-positive and question-negative pairs showed better separation than before training, though still with overlap.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Similarity-distribution separation is a cheap pre-deployment signal that fine-tuning worked.
insights.locator: This was a little bit about the distributed training at a high level.

insights.claim: On a golden set of 300 SME-verified questions, answers and sources, Dell's fine-tuned embedding model retrieved roughly 12% more correct sources (recall@k).
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Quantifies the payoff of domain-tuned embeddings: double-digit retrieval gains on enterprise jargon.
insights.locator: Said, ok, good signal, let's continue.

insights.claim: End-to-end answer quality measured by LLM-as-a-judge (question-to-answer relevance and answer-to-ground-truth match) improved by a little more than 4% with the fine-tuned embedding — characterized as a good improvement but not a great success.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Retrieval gains translate only partially into answer quality; expect modest end-user improvements from embedding fine-tuning alone.
insights.quote: Not a great success, but a very good improvement.
insights.locator: You take like more top 20.

insights.claim: Dell decides when to retrain its fine-tuned embedding model by monitoring the rate of data change (e.g., a million new Confluence pages in a month), data drift between training and production distributions, and user signals such as thumbs up/down and whether users click cited sources.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Fine-tuned models create an ongoing retraining and monitoring workload — recurring demand for MLOps and compute.
insights.locator: We said, ok, let's deploy it.

insights.claim: Embeddings are framed as an under-appreciated foundation of enterprise AI, with information retrieval via RAG the most common enterprise use, followed by classification, clustering and recommendation systems.
insights.speaker: Rachel Shalom
insights.so_what: Embedding quality is a quiet lever on enterprise AI ROI that attracts less attention than LLM choice.
insights.quote: I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked.
insights.locator: Summary
